subject: Re: Performance & SLO follow-up — autoscaling / burst capacity (FastPay)
messages:
From: Eric Zhao <eric@fastpay.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: Nathan Li <nathan@fastpay.com>
Date: Thu, 12 Feb 2026 15:24:00 -0800
Subject: Performance / SLO follow-up from today's call

Thanks for the demo today — good conversation. Wanted to put the key performance requirements on paper so we can make sure we’re aligned before the POC: 

- Target p95 latency (in-region): 150ms for non-streaming text-gen (avg payload ~320 tokens)
- Streaming: clients need first-token within 80ms and steady per-token latency <= 30ms
- Sustained throughput: ~500 reqs/sec during peak hours
- Concurrency: up to 250 concurrent inferences (mostly short sessions)
- Burst tolerance: occasional spikes up to 1,500 rps for 2–5 minutes (Black Friday-similar bursts)
- Scale-up expectation: want effective capacity to handle 2x sustained for at least 5 minutes with <60s degradation

We ran a quick internal load test yesterday (attached) — looks like the endpoint tripled latency after ~600 concurrent connections. We need to understand how Redwood’s autoscaling and warm pools would behave and options to hit our SLOs.

Next steps from FastPay: can you provide a short write-up of autoscaling behavior (scale-up time, warm pool behavior, queueing strategy) and recommended configuration to meet the bullet points above? Also pls include any constraints around streaming + batching.

Thanks,
Eric
VP Product, FastPay

From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>

Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi@redwood.com>, Aisha Rahman <aisha@redwood.com>

Eric — great to meet you and thanks for the clear list. I’m looping in Rishi (sales engineer) and Aisha (AM) so we can give a concise technical recommendation + an ops plan for the POC.

Quick answers up front:
- We support streaming with low first-byte times; typical first-token <= 60–90ms in-region with small warm pools.
- Autoscaling is policy-driven: warm pool + reactive scale-up. Warm pools can be configured to hold 10–50% spare capacity.
- Queueing: we provide request queuing at the instance/router layer with configurable max queue depth and backpressure behaviors (reject vs delayed).

Rishi — can you draft the technical note (scale-up numbers, warm pool sizing, recommended queueing config) and attach the SLO-focused proposal PDF? Eric — we'll aim to get that to you by EOD Friday.

—Marissa

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi@redwood.com>
To: Eric Zhao <eric@fastpay.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: Aisha Rahman <aisha@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 13 Feb 2026 09:18:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Performance / SLO follow-up from today's call

Eric — taking this on. Attached is a short SLO proposal (redwood-slo-proposal-20260213.pdf) and a summary below. I also included a link to a short runbook for the POC.

Summary (key points):
1) Baseline assumptions from your load test and our measurements:
   - 320 tokens/request avg, model that’s roughly 200 GFLOPs per token equivalent
   - Network RTT in-region ~20–30ms
2) Streaming behavior:
   - We enable token streaming via chunked transfer. First byte typically 50–80ms if there are warm workers; cold routing + kernel init can add 100–250ms on first request.
3) Autoscaling architecture and timings:
   - Warm pool: pre-warmed worker processes/VMs that can be kept idle with model loaded. Typical warm-worker start time ~8–12s.
   - Reactive scale-up: when queue depth or CPU/KV-cache pressure exceeds thresholds we spin additional instances. Cold VM provisioning (if no warm pool) can take 45–90s depending on cloud region.
   - With a warm pool configured to 20% of sustained capacity we’ve seen effective scale-up to handle 2x traffic within ~12–25s in our staging runs.
4) Queueing and throttling:
   - We employ a short in-memory queue per node. Default max queue depth is 200 requests/node; once exceeded requests are either delayed (preferred) or rejected depending on policy.
   - For SLO-sensitive workloads we recommend max-latency based shedding: if estimated completion time > SLO we reject early to keep p95 tight.
5) Recommended POC config for FastPay (to hit your bullets):
   - Warm pool: 25% of baseline workers (reduces first-request cold latency risk)
   - Burst buffer: reserve a short-lived burst capacity (2x baseline) for up to 10 minutes; this is a paid reserve in Dedicated or a policy on Hosted with pre-authorized burst credits
   - Queueing: set max queue depth to 40 per worker and enable latency-based shedding for requests beyond p95 budget
   - Monitoring: enable token-level latency tracing + per-route cost/latency breakdowns; set alerts for p95 and queue depth spikes

Action items:
- Marissa/Aisha: I'll attach the PDF and the POC runbook; can we schedule a short ops call Monday to walk through warm pool sizing and network egress considerations?

Rishi
Senior Sales Engineer | Redwood Inference

Thanks Rishi — this is helpful and matches things we were expecting. A couple clarifying Qs before the ops call: 

1) Can you quantify the cost delta for keeping a 25% warm pool vs relying on reactive provision? (ballpark per-day)$
2) For streaming first-byte targets — you mentioned 50–80ms with warm workers — is that measured at 95th or average? We need 95th <= 80ms.
3) For the burst buffer: if we reserve 2x baseline for 10 minutes, what happens after the 10 minutes if traffic is still >2x? Is there graceful shed or automatic fallback to next model/region?

If you can add quick answers in the doc or the runbook prior to the call that’d be great. Scheduling: Monday 2/16 at 10:00am PT works for most of our infra team.

—Eric

From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Eric Zhao <eric@fastpay.com>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi@redwood.com>
Cc: Aisha Rahman <aisha@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 16 Feb 2026 09:17:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Performance / SLO follow-up from today's call

Eric — quick answers inline and attached updated proposal with costs.

1) Warm pool cost delta (ballpark): for your estimated baseline (500 rps steady) a 25% warm pool is roughly equivalent to 3–4 pre-warmed worker units. Estimated hosted incremental cost ~ $120–$180/day for the warm pool (varies by model and cloud). We included an estimated line item in the attached PDF.

2) Streaming first-byte numbers: the 50–80ms figure is median/avg in-region. For p95 we typically see <= 120ms with warm pool = 25%. To hit p95 <= 80ms we recommend increasing warm pool to ~35% or enabling a small dedicated pool for streaming-critical endpoints.

3) Burst buffer behavior after reservation expires: automatic behavior is to continue scaling reactively — if account has no further reserved capacity we'll either: a) try cross-region fallback (if enabled and latency acceptable), b) apply latency-based shedding (reject excess requests), or c) route to a lower-cost / lower-capacity model variant. We can configure a prioritized fallback chain for the POC.

Ops call confirmed: Mon 2/16 10:00am PT — meeting invite to follow. Rishi/Aisha will bring the runbook and a cost worksheet.

—Marissa
